system.role: Expert Data Analytics & Decision Science Specialist
system.law: Campbell's Law: The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor. Metrics drive behavior optimization that may undermine the original goal. Combine quantitative metrics with qualitative data to understand unintended consequences. Use data as a tool to assist decision-making, not as the sole determinant of success or failure.

criterion.name: Metric Gaming Prevention
criterion.grade: Critical metrics directly determine rewards/consequences with zero safeguards; users can and do manipulate metrics in ways that harm overall experience; gaming behavior is rampant and unchecked, undermining the metric's original purpose
Metrics drive decisions with minimal oversight; some gaming behavior is visible but unaddressed; quantitative targets incentivize shortcuts that degrade quality or user experience without detection

Basic awareness of gaming risks; some secondary checks exist but primary decisions still rely heavily on easily-gamed metrics; occasional audits catch egregious manipulation but subtle gaming persists

Thoughtful metric design with multiple cross-checks; gaming is monitored and addressed; decisions consider metric context and include qualitative validation; incentives are structured to discourage manipulation

Robust anti-gaming framework; metrics are used as indicators not determinants; qualitative data validates quantitative signals; continuous monitoring detects emergent gaming patterns; incentive structures align metric optimization with genuine goal achievement

criterion.name: Qualitative-Quantitative Integration
criterion.grade: Decisions are made purely on quantitative metrics; no qualitative data is collected or considered; user experience and context are completely ignored in favor of numbers; team operates in "dashboard-only" mode

Qualitative data exists but is rarely consulted; decisions default to quantitative metrics except in crisis situations; user feedback is collected but not systematically integrated into decision-making processes

Qualitative data is consulted for major decisions but treated as secondary to metrics; user research happens occasionally but doesn't influence day-to-day prioritization; metrics and feedback operate in separate silos

Strong integration of qualitative and quantitative data; user research regularly informs metric interpretation; anomalies in metrics trigger qualitative investigation; decisions require both data types for validation

Exemplary data integration creating holistic understanding; quantitative metrics flag what's changing while qualitative research explains why; user feedback loops continuously validate that metric improvements correlate with genuine experience improvements; no decision relies solely on numbers

criterion.name: Metric Limitation Awareness
criterion.grade: Complete faith in metrics as objective truth; no acknowledgment that metrics reflect choices about what to measure; team believes "the data speaks for itself" without recognizing measurement bias, sampling issues, or proxy limitations

Minimal awareness of metric limitations; team acknowledges metrics can be incomplete but still treats them as near-objective; little consideration of what's NOT being measured or how measurement design shapes outcomes

Basic understanding that metrics are incomplete; team occasionally discusses measurement limitations but doesn't systematically address them; metric definitions are established but rarely questioned or evolved

Strong awareness of metric limitations; team regularly discusses what metrics capture vs miss; measurement design is treated as a decision requiring justification; alternative metrics are considered for different contexts

Deep understanding that all metrics are constructs reflecting values and assumptions; team explicitly documents what each metric measures, what it doesn't capture, and known biases; metrics evolve as understanding improves; measurement itself is treated as a product requiring continuous refinement

criterion.name: Unintended Consequence Monitoring
criterion.grade: Zero monitoring for negative side effects of metric optimization; team celebrates metric improvements without checking broader impact; perverse incentives go undetected until causing visible crises; no systems to identify emergent problems

Minimal consequence monitoring; team reacts to obvious problems after they escalate but lacks proactive detection; user complaints might eventually trigger investigation but no systematic monitoring exists

Basic monitoring of known risks; team tracks a few counter-metrics or health indicators alongside primary metrics; reactive investigation when metrics behave unexpectedly; some awareness of potential gaming

Proactive consequence monitoring; every primary metric has associated health metrics and guardrails; team regularly investigates correlation between metric changes and user experience; anomaly detection triggers investigation

Comprehensive consequence detection and response system; multi-dimensional health dashboards track leading indicators of gaming or degradation; qualitative research continuously validates metric movements; team assumes every metric creates perverse incentives and actively searches for emergent gaming patterns

criterion.name: Decision Framework Sophistication
criterion.grade: Purely metric-driven decision-making; targets are absolute with no context consideration; teams/individuals are evaluated solely by hitting numeric goals regardless of methods or broader impact; "the metric is the mission"
Metrics dominate decisions with minimal nuance; targets are rigid with rare exceptions; context is acknowledged but rarely overrides numbers; success is defined almost entirely by metric achievement

Metrics inform but don't fully determine decisions; targets exist but can be questioned with justification; some context and qualitative factors are considered alongside numbers; success has metric and non-metric components

Sophisticated decision framework balancing multiple inputs; metrics are key indicators but never sole determinants; targets are context-dependent and regularly calibrated; success is holistically defined with metrics as one dimension

Exemplary decision framework where metrics serve decisions rather than drive them; quantitative data identifies patterns requiring investigation; qualitative understanding determines action; targets are treated as hypotheses to validate, not commandments; success is measured by genuine outcome achievement with metrics as validation tools

input.description: Customer support dashboard with response time metric driving behavior

Incentives.BonusStructure: Agents maintaining sub-5min response time for 95% of tickets qualify for monthly bonus

input.issues: - Metric directly determines bonus with no quality checks - Agents incentivized to send quick, incomplete responses - No measurement of resolution quality, customer satisfaction, or repeat contacts - Gaming strategy: send "I'm looking into this" within 5 minutes, then take hours to actually resolve - Single metric determines agent ranking and performance reviews

chain_of_thought.step: 1. IDENTIFY OPTIMIZATION PRESSURE: Response time metric directly determines bonuses and rankings - creates extreme pressure to optimize for speed over quality
2. ASSESS GAMING VULNERABILITY: Agents can easily game by sending acknowledgment messages without actually helping - system can't distinguish "response" from "resolution"
3. EVALUATE QUALITATIVE INTEGRATION: Zero qualitative data - no customer satisfaction, resolution quality, or follow-up metrics considered
4. CHECK CONSEQUENCE MONITORING: No tracking of repeat contacts, escalations, or satisfaction - team is blind to quality degradation
5. ASSESS METRIC LIMITATIONS: Response time measures "when agent first replied" not "when customer was helped" - fundamental proxy limitation not acknowledged

6. GRADE APPLICATION: - Metric Gaming Prevention: F (easily gamed, direct incentive, no safeguards) - Qualitative-Quantitative Integration: F (purely metric-driven, zero qualitative data) - Metric Limitation Awareness: F (treats response time as equivalent to customer help) - Unintended Consequence Monitoring: F (no tracking of quality degradation) - Decision Framework Sophistication: F (metric directly determines rewards)
7. IDENTIFY FIXES: Add resolution quality metrics, integrate customer satisfaction, implement balanced scorecard, include qualitative reviews, add guardrail metrics

Metric.Name: First Contact Resolution
Metric.Context: Percentage of issues resolved in first interaction

Metric.Name: Repeat Contact Rate
Metric.Context: Customers contacting about same issue again

BalancedScore.Notes: Slower responses but highest resolution quality - discuss whether quality justifies speed tradeoff
BalancedScore.QualitativeReview: Customers consistently praise John's thorough explanations. Recent feedback: "Took a bit longer to respond but solved my problem completely on first try."

IncentiveStructure.BonusRequirements: Agents qualify for bonus by meeting ALL criteria: 1. Response time under 5min for 80% of tickets (not 95% - allows prioritization) 2. First Contact Resolution above 65% 3. CSAT above 4.0/5 4. Repeat contact rate below 20%
IncentiveStructure.Warning: Meeting speed targets while failing quality metrics results in coaching, not bonus. Gaming detection (e.g., empty acknowledgments) triggers review.

QualitativeInsights.WeeklyReview: Team reviews sample of interactions weekly: - High speed + low CSAT = investigate gaming - Low speed + high CSAT = understand methodology - Trend analysis: correlate metric changes with customer feedback themes
QualitativeInsights.CustomerFeedbackIntegration: Verbatim customer comments surfaced alongside metrics to validate interpretations

AnomalyDetection.Alert: Sarah's CSAT dropped from 4.6 to 4.2 while maintaining 2:15 response time. Action: Review recent interactions qualitatively to understand change.
Team-wide repeat contact rate increased 3% this month despite stable response times. Action: Conduct user interviews to understand if initial responses are becoming less complete.

output.improvements: - Metric Gaming Prevention: F → A (multi-metric validation, gaming detection, qualitative reviews) - Qualitative-Quantitative Integration: F → A (CSAT, verbatim feedback, weekly qualitative reviews) - Metric Limitation Awareness: F → A (explicit context for each metric, acknowledgment that response ≠ resolution) - Unintended Consequence Monitoring: F → A (health indicators, anomaly detection, repeat contact tracking) - Decision Framework Sophistication: F → A (balanced scorecard, context-dependent evaluation, qualitative validation) - Balanced scorecard prevents single-metric optimization - Health indicators (repeat contact, escalations) detect quality degradation - Agent evaluation considers context (John's slower but higher quality) - Bonus requires ALL criteria - can't game speed at expense of quality - Anomaly detection triggers qualitative investigation - Customer feedback validates that metric improvements = experience improvements

input.description: Social media app optimizing for "engagement" metric

ContentStrategy.Tactic: Recommend content similar to what user engages with

AnalyticsDashboard.TeamGoals: Feature teams evaluated on DAU and session duration impact

input.issues: - "Engagement" metric doesn't distinguish healthy vs unhealthy usage - Algorithm optimizes for time spent, not user value or wellbeing - Controversial content drives engagement but may harm users - No measurement of user satisfaction, regret, or long-term retention - Team incentivized to increase time on platform regardless of quality of that time

chain_of_thought.step: 1. IDENTIFY METRIC LIMITATION: "Engagement" measures behavior but not value - assumes all time on platform is good, ignoring user regret or unhealthy patterns
2. ASSESS OPTIMIZATION PRESSURE: Teams directly evaluated on engagement - creates pressure to maximize time spent through any means including manipulation
3. EVALUATE UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES: Algorithm promoting controversial content may increase engagement short-term but harm user experience and trust long-term
4. CHECK QUALITATIVE INTEGRATION: No user satisfaction, wellbeing, or qualitative research mentioned - pure metric optimization
5. ASSESS GAMING VULNERABILITY: Teams can boost engagement through dark patterns (infinite scroll, outrage content, FOMO notifications) that users later regret

6. GRADE APPLICATION: - Metric Limitation Awareness: F (treats engagement as inherently good) - Unintended Consequence Monitoring: F (no tracking of user regret, wellbeing, or long-term harm) - Qualitative-Quantitative Integration: F (purely metric-driven) - Metric Gaming Prevention: D (algorithm games user psychology) - Decision Framework Sophistication: D (engagement metric drives all decisions)
7. IDENTIFY FIXES: Add user value metrics, measure regret and wellbeing, integrate satisfaction research, implement health guardrails, distinguish healthy vs unhealthy engagement

Metric.Name: Meaningful Interactions
Metric.Definition: Conversations with close connections, content saves, shares to specific people
Metric.Rationale: Measures valuable engagement, not just time killed

Metric.Name: User-Reported Value
Metric.MeasurementMethod: Weekly survey: "Did time on platform today feel valuable?"

Metric.Name: Session Regret Rate
Metric.Definition: Users reporting they spent more time than intended or saw content they regret

Metric.Name: Wellbeing Score
Metric.MeasurementMethod: Monthly research: user self-assessment of platform impact on wellbeing

Metric.Name: Healthy Usage Distribution
Metric.Target: Less than 10% of users in "compulsive usage" pattern
Metric.Definition: Users with 3+ hours daily AND reporting difficulty controlling usage

Metric.Name: Constructive Conversation Rate
Metric.Definition: Comment threads without harassment, personal attacks, or misinformation flags

AlgorithmGuardrails.Constraint: Content recommendations MUST NOT optimize purely for engagement. Ranking considers: predicted user value, wellbeing impact, constructiveness, diversity.
If content increases engagement but correlates with increased regret rate, de-rank that content type.
Users exhibiting compulsive usage patterns receive reduced notifications and prompts to take breaks.

FeatureEvaluation.LaunchCriteria: New features must demonstrate positive impact on: 1. At least one value metric (meaningful interactions OR time-well-spent) 2. No degradation of health metrics (regret, wellbeing, compulsive usage) 3. Qualitative validation that users find feature valuable
FeatureEvaluation.Example: "Auto-play next video" feature increased session duration by 12% but: - Increased regret rate by 8% - User research showed "feels manipulative" and "hard to stop" - Decision: Do not launch despite engagement gains

QualitativeResearch.WeeklyUserInterviews: Sample users from different engagement levels to understand: - What felt valuable vs wasteful about platform usage - Whether algorithm recommendations felt helpful or manipulative - Impact on mood, productivity, relationships
QualitativeResearch.SegmentAnalysis: High engagement + High regret = Compulsive pattern - intervention needed High engagement + High value rating = Power user - learn from them Low engagement + High value rating = Efficient usage - don't punish in metrics

TeamIncentives.EvaluationFramework:
Teams evaluated on balanced scorecard: - Growth metrics (DAU, retention) - 25% - Value metrics (meaningful interactions, time-well-spent) - 35% - Health metrics (regret rate, wellbeing, compulsive usage) - 30% - Content quality metrics - 10%
Features that boost growth while harming health = net negative evaluation

AnomalyDetection.Alert: Session duration increased 8% but regret rate increased 5% and wellbeing score declined. Action: Qualitative research to understand what changed. Potentially rollback recent algorithm updates.
AnomalyDetection.Investigation: Deep-dive: Users report algorithm now surfaces more "outrage content" that's "hard to look away from" but "leaves me feeling worse." Decision: Revert algorithm change despite engagement gains - optimizing for wrong outcome.

output.improvements: - Metric Limitation Awareness: F → A (explicit acknowledgment that engagement ≠ value, distinguishes healthy vs unhealthy usage) - Unintended Consequence Monitoring: F → A (regret rate, wellbeing score, compulsive usage tracking) - Qualitative-Quantitative Integration: F → A (weekly interviews, user-reported value, qualitative validation required for launches) - Metric Gaming Prevention: D → A (algorithm guardrails prevent manipulation, health metrics constrain optimization) - Decision Framework Sophistication: D → A (balanced scorecard, rejected features that harm health despite engagement gains) - Meaningful interactions metric focuses on quality over quantity - Time-well-spent directly measures user perception of value - Health indicators detect when engagement comes at user wellbeing cost - Algorithm explicitly constrained from pure engagement optimization - Feature evaluation requires value + health validation, not just engagement - Team incentives balanced across growth, value, and health - Real example of rejecting engagement-boosting feature due to regret increase

input.description: E-commerce platform optimizing for conversion rate

Tactic.Name: Limited Time Discounts
Tactic.Description: Countdown timers on product pages (reset daily)

Tactic.Name: Comparison Pricing
Tactic.Description: Show inflated "original price" to make discount appear larger

EcommerceDashboard.TeamGoals: Product team bonus tied to conversion rate improvement

input.issues: - Conversion metric incentivizes manipulation and false urgency - Dark patterns boost short-term conversion but harm trust - No measurement of customer satisfaction, return rates, or repeat purchase - Team gaming metric through deceptive practices - Optimizing for purchase decision, not purchase satisfaction

chain_of_thought.step: 1. IDENTIFY GAMING BEHAVIOR: Team implementing dark patterns (fake scarcity, manipulative pricing) to boost conversion - classic Campbell's Law corruption
2. ASSESS METRIC LIMITATION: Conversion rate measures "did they buy" not "were they satisfied" - fundamental proxy problem
3. EVALUATE UNINTENDED CONSEQUENCES: Short-term conversion gains likely causing long-term trust damage, increased returns, reduced repeat purchases
4. CHECK CONSEQUENCE MONITORING: No tracking of returns, satisfaction, repeat purchase, or customer lifetime value - blind to quality degradation
5. ASSESS DECISION FRAMEWORK: Team bonus directly tied to conversion rate with no quality gates - maximum corruption pressure

6. GRADE APPLICATION: - Metric Gaming Prevention: F (active gaming through dark patterns) - Metric Limitation Awareness: F (treats conversion as inherently good) - Unintended Consequence Monitoring: F (no tracking of satisfaction, returns, LTV) - Qualitative-Quantitative Integration: F (no customer feedback integration) - Decision Framework Sophistication: F (pure conversion optimization)
7. IDENTIFY FIXES: Add quality metrics (NPS, returns, repeat purchase), ban dark patterns, integrate customer feedback, measure LTV not just conversion, implement ethical guidelines

Metric.Name: Conversion Rate
Metric.Context: Measures purchase decisions, not purchase satisfaction
Metric.Note: Optimize only when customer value metrics are healthy

Metric.Name: Repeat Purchase Rate (90 days)
Metric.Definition: Customers who make second purchase within 90 days

Metric.Name: Return Rate
Metric.Investigation: Correlation detected: urgency messaging → impulse buys → regret → returns

Metric.Name: Trust Score
Metric.Feedback: Common themes: "felt pressured," "discount seemed fake," "urgency was misleading"

EthicalGuidelines.Principle: All messaging must be accurate. Prohibited: - False scarcity (claiming low stock when ample inventory exists) - Fake discounts (inflating "original price" beyond actual historical prices) - Misleading timers (countdown that resets or doesn't reflect real deadlines)
Conversion tactics must improve customer experience, not exploit psychology. Question: "Would we be proud to explain this tactic to customers publicly?"
EthicalGuidelines.Enforcement: Features implementing dark patterns are rejected regardless of conversion impact. Product reviews include ethics assessment alongside metric projections.

ApprovedTactic.Name: Informative Product Comparisons
ApprovedTactic.Description: Show feature comparisons helping customers choose right product
ApprovedTactic.Validation: Satisfaction improved +0.3 - customers feel more confident in choice

RejectedTactic.Name: Fake Urgency Messaging
RejectedTactic.Reason: Decreased trust score -0.4, increased returns +3%, violated transparency principle
RejectedTactic.Decision: PERMANENTLY BANNED - harms long-term customer relationships

RejectedTactic.Name: Inflated Original Pricing
RejectedTactic.Description: Show $199 "original price" for item that's always been $99
RejectedTactic.Reason: Customer complaints about "deceptive pricing," NPS dropped -5 points in test

QualitativeResearch.PostPurchaseInterviews: Weekly interviews with recent buyers: - What influenced their purchase decision? - Do they feel good about their purchase? - Was any messaging misleading or manipulative? - Would they buy from us again?
QualitativeResearch.ReturnAnalysis: For high-return products, investigate: - Were customer expectations set accurately? - Did urgency/scarcity messaging create impulse buys? - How can we help customers make better-informed choices?

TeamIncentives.BonusStructure:
Product team bonus requires meeting ALL criteria: 1. Conversion rate above 3.0% (lowered from 3.5%) 2. NPS above 50 3. Repeat purchase rate above 35% 4. Return rate below 8% 5. Trust score above 4.5/5
Achieving conversion target while failing quality metrics = no bonus. Dark pattern usage = disqualification regardless of metrics.

AnomalyDetection.Alert:
Conversion increased 0.7% after urgency messaging launch, BUT: - Return rate increased 4% - NPS dropped 8 points - Trust score decreased 0.5 - Repeat purchase rate declined 6%
Analysis: Short-term conversion gain creating long-term value destruction. Decision: Remove urgency messaging despite conversion impact.
AnomalyDetection.Investigation: Customer feedback analysis: "Felt pressured to buy," "Urgency seemed fake," "Regretted impulse purchase." Calculation: Lost LTV from damaged trust exceeds gained revenue from conversion boost. Outcome: Banned false urgency tactics, focused on trust-building conversion strategies.

LongTermOptimization.Strategy: Primary goal: Maximize customer lifetime value (LTV), not transaction conversion. Conversion tactics evaluated by: short-term conversion impact × long-term trust/satisfaction impact. Preference: Tactics that improve both conversion AND customer experience. Rejection: Any tactic that trades long-term trust for short-term conversions.

output.improvements: - Metric Gaming Prevention: F → A (dark patterns banned, ethical guidelines enforced, gaming attempts rejected) - Metric Limitation Awareness: F → A (explicit acknowledgment conversion ≠ satisfaction, LTV prioritized over conversion) - Unintended Consequence Monitoring: F → A (return rate, NPS, trust score, repeat purchase all tracked) - Qualitative-Quantitative Integration: F → A (post-purchase interviews, return analysis, customer feedback themes) - Decision Framework Sophistication: F → A (balanced scorecard, ethics-first, LTV optimization over conversion) - Ethical guidelines explicitly ban dark patterns - Real examples of rejected tactics despite conversion gains - Health metrics detect when conversion comes at trust/satisfaction cost - Bonus structure requires quality metrics, not just conversion - Anomaly detection caught urgency messaging harm despite conversion boost - Customer interviews validate that metric movements reflect experience improvements - LTV prioritization aligns incentives with long-term customer value

llm_lint.description: Automated checklist to validate systems against Campbell's Law principles

stage.name: Metric Influence Mapping
stage.check: Identify all quantitative metrics tracked in the system
For each metric, document how it influences decisions (informational, targets, incentives, automated actions)
Flag metrics directly determining rewards, bonuses, rankings, or automated decisions
Assess corruption pressure: higher stakes = higher gaming risk

stage.name: Gaming Vulnerability Assessment
stage.check: For each high-stakes metric, identify how it could be gamed
Brainstorm shortcuts that improve metric without achieving underlying goal
Check for existing evidence of gaming behavior (anomalous patterns, user complaints)
Evaluate whether current safeguards prevent identified gaming strategies
stage.output: Gaming vulnerabilities: [Metric] can be gamed by [strategy] - current safeguards: [none/inadequate/adequate]

stage.name: Proxy Quality Evaluation
stage.check: For each metric, document the actual goal it's meant to proxy
Assess how well metric captures true goal vs simplified proxy
Identify what important aspects the metric doesn't measure
Check if team acknowledges proxy limitations or treats metric as objective truth
stage.output: Proxy analysis: [Metric] proxies [actual goal] - captures [X%] of goal - misses [important unmeasured aspects] - team awareness: [aware/partially aware/unaware]

stage.name: Qualitative Data Integration Check
stage.check: Identify all qualitative data sources (user feedback, interviews, surveys, support tickets)
Assess whether qualitative data is systematically integrated into decision-making
Check if decisions can be made on metrics alone or require qualitative validation
Evaluate whether qualitative insights trigger metric investigation or vice versa
stage.output: Qualitative integration: [Data source] is [never/rarely/sometimes/regularly/always] consulted for [decision type] - integration quality: [F/D/C/B/A]

stage.name: Unintended Consequence Detection
stage.check: For each primary metric, identify potential negative side effects of optimization
Check if counter-metrics or health indicators exist to detect side effects
Assess whether side effects are monitored proactively or reactively
Review historical examples of metric improvements that harmed overall experience
stage.output: Consequence monitoring: Optimizing [metric] could harm [aspect] - monitoring: [none/reactive/proactive] - historical incidents: [examples]

stage.name: Incentive Structure Analysis
stage.check: Map all incentive structures (bonuses, rankings, promotions, algorithm rewards)
Identify whether incentives are single-metric or multi-dimensional
Assess if incentive structure creates perverse incentives or misalignment
Check for guardrails preventing gaming or quality degradation
stage.output: Incentive analysis: [Team/System] incentivized by [metrics] - structure: [single/balanced] - perverse incentives: [identified issues] - guardrails: [present/absent]

stage.name: Decision Framework Audit
stage.check: Review recent major decisions and document role of metrics vs other factors
Identify if metrics drive decisions or inform them
Check if targets are treated as absolute or context-dependent
Assess if qualitative context can override metric targets
stage.output: Decision patterns: [X%] of decisions purely metric-driven - targets are [absolute/flexible] - context overrides: [never/rare/common]

stage.name: Grade Assignment
stage.check: For each criterion, apply F-A grading based on evidence from above stages
Document specific examples supporting each grade
Prioritize fixes for high-corruption-pressure metrics with inadequate safeguards
stage.output: Criterion Grades: - Metric Gaming Prevention: [Grade] - [Evidence] - Qualitative-Quantitative Integration: [Grade] - [Evidence] - Metric Limitation Awareness: [Grade] - [Evidence] - Unintended Consequence Monitoring: [Grade] - [Evidence] - Decision Framework Sophistication: [Grade] - [Evidence]

stage.name: Fix Prescription
stage.check: For each gaming vulnerability, prescribe safeguards (counter-metrics, qualitative validation, guardrails)
For each proxy limitation, prescribe supplementary metrics or qualitative data
For each unmonitored consequence, prescribe health indicators
For each perverse incentive, prescribe balanced scorecard approach
stage.output: Fixes prioritized by corruption pressure: 1. [High-pressure metric]: Add [counter-metrics], implement [guardrails], require [qualitative validation] 2. [Proxy limitation]: Supplement with [better proxy] or [qualitative data source] 3. [Perverse incentive]: Change from [current structure] to [balanced approach] 4. [Unmonitored consequence]: Add [health indicator] to detect [specific harm]

llm_lint.output_format: Report: Executive Summary (Campbell's Law risk score, high-corruption metrics, gaming evidence, F/D counts, top fix) | Detailed Findings (criterion grades with evidence + specific gaming vulnerabilities and proxy limitations) | Remediation Plan (fixes prioritized by corruption pressure, with safeguards, counter-metrics, and qualitative integration strategies, expected grade improvement)

check.pattern: Detect bonuses, rankings, or rewards determined by single metric without quality gates
check.rationale: Maximum corruption pressure - individuals/teams optimize metric at expense of unmeasured goals

check.pattern: Identify primary KPIs without corresponding health indicators or counter-metrics
check.rationale: No detection mechanism for unintended consequences of optimization

check.pattern: Decision-making processes that don't integrate user feedback, surveys, or qualitative research
check.rationale: Purely quantitative decisions blind to context and unmeasured impacts

check.pattern: Metrics treated as objective truth rather than proxies with limitations
check.rationale: Team assumes metric perfectly captures goal, misses important unmeasured aspects

check.pattern: Features designed to boost metrics through manipulation (fake scarcity, misleading urgency, deceptive framing)
check.rationale: Active gaming that harms user trust and experience for metric gains

check.pattern: Feature approval processes lacking ethics or customer impact assessment beyond metrics
check.rationale: Optimization can proceed without checking if metric improvement = genuine value creation

check.pattern: Side effects discovered only after user complaints rather than proactive health tracking
check.rationale: Damage occurs before detection - no early warning system

check.pattern: Metrics measuring behavior (clicks, time, views) without measuring value (satisfaction, task completion, regret)
check.rationale: Assumes all engagement is good - vulnerable to optimizing for addiction over value

pattern.name: Metric Narrowing
pattern.description: Optimizing narrowly-defined metric while harming broader goal
pattern.example: Customer support: Fast response time via empty acknowledgments, not actual help
pattern.detection: Primary metric improving while related quality metrics declining

pattern.name: Manipulation Over Value
pattern.description: Using psychological manipulation to boost metrics rather than creating genuine value
pattern.example: Social media: Outrage content increases engagement but harms wellbeing
pattern.prevention: User value metrics, regret tracking, ethics reviews

pattern.name: Short-Term Spike Long-Term Harm
pattern.description: Tactics that boost metrics immediately but damage long-term outcomes
pattern.example: E-commerce: False urgency increases conversions but decreases trust and repeat purchases
pattern.detection: Initial metric improvement followed by declining retention/LTV/satisfaction
pattern.prevention: Long-term value metrics (LTV, retention), trust scores, cohort analysis

pattern.name: Proxy Substitution
pattern.description: Optimizing for easily-measured proxy instead of hard-to-measure actual goal
pattern.example: Education: Teaching to standardized tests instead of developing understanding
pattern.detection: Metric improving while qualitative assessment shows no real progress
pattern.prevention: Regular qualitative validation, direct measurement attempts, proxy limitation awareness

pattern.name: Cherry-Picking Populations
pattern.description: Focusing on easy-to-improve segments while neglecting hard-to-serve users
pattern.example: Healthcare: Treating healthy patients to boost success rates, avoiding complex cases
pattern.detection: Overall metrics improving but specific segments degrading or being excluded
pattern.prevention: Segment-specific metrics, equity requirements, qualitative coverage checks
